summary:
FieldShift AI is an AI-powered agricultural decision-support platform that helps farmers make climate-informed crop and crop-rotation decisions using NASA Earth observation data.

The platform combines NASA datasets, including POWER, GPM IMERG, SMAP, ECOSTRESS and Harmonized Landsat Sentinel-2 (HLS), with soil information, crop characteristics and farmer priorities. It analyzes weather patterns, rainfall, soil moisture, evapotranspiration, evaporative stress and vegetation indicators to provide location-specific environmental insights. Farmers can explore their fields, understand environmental conditions, evaluate crop suitability and compare multi-season crop rotation strategies through an interactive dashboard.

FieldShift AI addresses the challenge of adapting agriculture to changing climate and water conditions by transforming complex satellite observations into understandable, actionable information. It aims to help farmers identify environmental risks, make more informed crop choices, use water resources more thoughtfully and plan resilient farming systems.

By making NASA Earth science more accessible to agricultural decision-making, FieldShift AI bridges the gap between satellite technology and practical farming needs.
details:
Project Details — FieldShift AI

FieldShift AI is an AI-powered agricultural decision-support platform designed to help farmers adapt to changing climate and environmental conditions. It combines NASA Earth observation data with soil information, crop characteristics and farmer preferences to generate location-specific agricultural insights.

1. What does it do and how does it work?

Farmers can select their farm location or define their field boundary on an interactive map. The platform gathers environmental information from NASA datasets, including POWER, GPM IMERG, SMAP, ECOSTRESS and Harmonized Landsat Sentinel-2 (HLS). It analyzes weather patterns, rainfall, soil moisture, evapotranspiration, evaporative stress and vegetation indicators such as NDVI and NDWI. These insights support crop suitability recommendations and multi-season crop rotation planning. An AI assistant helps make complex environmental information easier to understand.

2. What benefits does it have?

  • Provides location-specific environmental and agricultural insights.
  • Helps farmers evaluate suitable crops and crop rotation strategies.
  • Makes satellite-derived information easier to understand.
  • Supports more informed water and resource management decisions.
  • Helps identify potential environmental stresses and agricultural risks.

3. What is the intended impact?

Our goal is to bridge the gap between NASA Earth science and practical farming decisions. FieldShift AI aims to strengthen climate resilience, encourage informed agricultural planning, improve awareness of changing environmental conditions and support more sustainable farming practices, particularly in rural and semi-urban communities.

4. What tools, languages and software were used?

  • Frontend: React 19, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS.
  • Backend: Node.js, Express.js and TypeScript.
  • AI: Google Gemini through the Google GenAI SDK.
  • Mapping and visualization: Leaflet, React-Leaflet and Recharts.
  • Data sources: NASA POWER, GPM IMERG, SMAP, ECOSTRESS and Landsat/HLS.
  • Data processing: GeoJSON-based farm boundaries, satellite observation processing, quality filtering, spatial analysis and caching.
  • Development environment: Google AI Studio Build Apps and standard development tools.

No specialized physical hardware is required; the platform is designed to work through a web application.

5. How is the project creative?

FieldShift AI creatively combines multiple NASA Earth observation datasets into a unified agricultural decision-support workflow. Instead of presenting satellite measurements as isolated scientific data, it connects environmental indicators with crop suitability and crop rotation planning. It also combines deterministic agricultural analysis with AI-powered explanations, helping users understand not only the recommendations but also the environmental evidence behind them.

6. What factors did the team consider?

We considered climate variability, rainfall patterns, water availability, soil conditions, vegetation health, crop requirements, seasonal changes and farmer priorities. We also prioritized data reliability, satellite observation quality, spatial coverage, acquisition dates and missing-data handling. Importantly, satellite-derived indicators are treated as supporting evidence rather than direct replacements for field measurements or laboratory soil tests. The system is designed to communicate data limitations and avoid presenting uncertain observations as definitive facts.
